design_detail: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR; protocol registered on the Open Science Framework) of human studies in which music was combined with ketamine or esketamine, in any population, dose, route or setting except recreational use. Five databases searched by a biomedical librarian (to December 2023) plus Google Scholar; 14 studies included: 5 with ketamine or esketamine alone (a case report, a two-patient case report, two qualitative studies and one controlled trial in children under anaesthesia) and 9 in which ketamine was given with other drugs for anaesthesia, sedation or transport. Studies were charted and, for the five ketamine-alone studies, themes were drawn inductively; included studies were not appraised and nothing was pooled.
can_establish: How much and what kind of research existed by December 2023 on music given with ketamine or esketamine (14 studies, mostly anaesthesia and sedation with other drugs; no study comparing music with no music during subanaesthetic ketamine for depression), and what those studies reported.
cannot_establish: Whether music reduces dissociation, anxiety, pain or sedative needs, or improves tolerability or antidepressant response, with ketamine or esketamine: the included studies were not appraised, most lack a no-music control or give ketamine with other drugs, and nothing was pooled.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (scoping review). 14 included studies with about 1,029 participants in total by the editors' sum of the Ns in Tables 1 and 2: 78 in the five ketamine-alone studies (1, 46, 2, 17 and 12) and 951 in the nine combination studies (107, 50, 33, 100, 50, 80, 490, 1 and 40).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: English-language peer-reviewed studies of the impact of combining ketamine or esketamine with music, in healthy volunteers or patients of any age, any indication, dose, route, order of drug and music, or type of music; individual case studies allowed. Excluded: non-music sounds, music videos, ketamine use in recreational settings (raves, parties, festivals), animal studies, conference material, abstracts, notes, book chapters and reviews, and studies in which music was only recommended or its effects not reported (Methods › 2.3. Eligibility Criteria, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.selection_effects: Restricted to English. Most of what exists concerns anaesthetic or sedative use in surgical, catheterization, endoscopy and air-transport settings, often in children, with ketamine given alongside other sedatives; recreational use was excluded by design, so the review says nothing about music where people use ketamine outside clinics.

exposure.measurement: Music as described by the included studies: patient-chosen music, investigator-selected instrumental or classical music, classical Indian music, pop music, and recordings of mothers' voices (singing, talking or praying), mostly through headphones, before, during and/or after ketamine (Tables 1 and 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as tabulated by the review: subanaesthetic intravenous ketamine (0.5 and 0.8 mg/kg) and intranasal or oral esketamine in the depression and alcohol-use-disorder studies; anaesthetic or sedative intravenous, oral or unspecified ketamine in the procedural studies (Tables 1 and 2).
exposure.polysubstance: In 9 of the 14 studies ketamine was given with other drugs (midazolam, fentanyl, propofol, morphine, promethazine, diazepam, glycopyrrolate, droperidol, hydromorphone, opioids and benzodiazepines), so music's effect with ketamine itself cannot be separated there (Table 2; 3.3, 1st to 8th paragraphs).

comparison.controls: Varies by study: no music through headphones or a blank soundtrack in most procedural trials; no control in the case reports and the qualitative studies; one study (Kudoh and Matsuki, 1999) compared two drug regimens that both had music (Tables 1 and 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the review; the primary studies' baseline comparability was not extracted or appraised.

outcomes.instruments: As charted: preoperative and postoperative anxiety, pain, fear, emergence reactions and agitation, dreams, sedative and analgesic requirements, vital signs, auditory evoked potentials, and qualitative accounts of dissociation, auditory distortion and tolerability (Tables 1 and 2).
outcomes.operationalization: Effects of music are reported as each study's own direction of findings; the review sets no outcome definitions.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to the review. Table 2 has a column on whether ketamine was given open label, which mixes the blinding of ketamine with the blinding of music allocation.

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled or computed; directions only, with one count: no additional sedatives were needed in 18 of 25 children who heard music against 5 of 25 who heard a blank soundtrack (Patil et al., 2014, as charted; Table 2). Other charted results: lower preoperative anxiety and fewer emergence reactions with maternal-voice recordings in 23 against 23 children (Kim et al., 2010); less intraoperative sedation and lower postoperative anxiety with music (de Araújo Azi et al., 2021); lower pain, fear, anxiety and vital signs after catheterization with classical or self-selected music than with none, and no difference between the two kinds of music (Karakul et al., 2022); lower anxiety and pain with patient-selected music during endoscopy sedation (Bay et al., 2021); no unpleasant dreams with music but no effect on emergence reactions (Kumar et al., 1992); more dreams or emergence reactions with music but none unpleasant against 10 controls with unpleasant dreams (Ambesh et al., 1991); lower ketamine and other drug use and lower pain with music and noise-cancelling headphones (34 against 85 and 371 patients; Gochenour et al., 2020).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Protocol written a priori with PRISMA-ScR as a guide and registered on the Open Science Framework (doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/ZYXPD) (Methods › 2.1. Protocol and Registration). The protocol was not read for this card, so deviations were not checked; the qualitative theme analysis of five studies is described as added (2.5).
analysis.selective_reporting: The Highlights list only benefits; the null and unfavourable findings reported in the body (no effect on emergence reactions in one trial, more dreams or emergence reactions with music in another, distortions experienced as negative, a patient who stopped the music) are left out of them.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Fourteen studies by December 2023: five with ketamine or esketamine alone (one controlled trial in 46 children under anaesthesia with maternal-voice recordings, a single-case report, a two-case report and two qualitative studies) and nine in which ketamine was combined with other sedatives or analgesics during procedures. No study comparing music with no music during subanaesthetic ketamine or esketamine for depression was found, and no included study was appraised.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Limitations say that no associations could be investigated and no conclusions drawn (5.0, 1st paragraph). The Highlights nevertheless state that with ketamine alone music reduces dissociation and anxiety and boosts tolerability, and that in combination studies it promotes relaxation and reduces sedative load; section 3.3 ends by suggesting that music interacts synergistically with anaesthetic agents including ketamine (3.3, 9th paragraph), and section 3.4 that music has the potential to effectively alleviate anxiety, stress and dissociative symptoms (3.4, 2nd paragraph). The recommendations tell clinicians to emphasize that calming instrumental music “is known to promote introspection and positive therapeutic outcomes” in ketamine sessions (4.0, 2nd recommendation), citing sources outside the included studies. The Introduction and Table 3 credit Kaelen et al. (2018) with showing that music improved psilocybin outcomes, which that correlational study did not test.

timeline.event: Kaelen et al. (2018), cited in the Introduction and Table 3 as showing that music improved psilocybin outcomes and brain emotional responses; it is a correlational mixed-methods study of 19 patients with no music-free condition and no brain measures (appraised in this round).

Primary ketamine-alone studies charted by the review: Greenway et al. (2021, two patients with bipolar depression), Mollaahmetoglu et al. (2021, qualitative, 12 people in a ketamine trial for alcohol use disorder) and Pereira et al. (2021, one patient on esketamine nasal spray); Breeksema et al. (2022, qualitative, 17 people on oral esketamine). Not read for this card.

Greenway et al. (2024), randomized clinical trial of music with ketamine for depression (haemodynamic response), on the project's BeforeDuring list; dated after this review's last search (December 2023) and not among its 14 studies (not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: A map, not an appraisal: up to December 2023 the evidence on music with ketamine came mostly from small procedural trials in which ketamine was combined with other sedatives, plus case reports and qualitative studies in depression and alcohol use disorder. Claims about benefits of music with ketamine must cite the primary studies after appraisal, and the later randomized trial (Greenway et al., 2024).

funding.funder: Funded in part by the German Research Foundation (DFG, 499724048, to MK), the Intramural Research Program of the National Institute of Mental Health, NIH (ZIAMH002857, to CAZ), and the NIH Library, Office of Research Services, in support of the NIH Intramural Research Program (AAL); the funders had no further role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit (Funding and Role of Funding Source).
funding.declared_conflicts: Carlos A. Zarate Jr is a co-inventor on a patent for the use of ketamine in major depression and suicidal ideation, on a patent for (2R,6R)-hydroxynorketamine, (S)-dehydronorketamine and other ketamine metabolites in depression and neuropathic pain, and on a patent application for (2R,6R)- and (2S,6S)-hydroxynorketamine in depression, anxiety, anhedonia, suicidal ideation and post-traumatic stress disorder; he has assigned his patent rights to the US government but will share a percentage of any royalties received by the government. All other authors declare no conflicts (Footnotes › Declaration of Interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the NIMH Experimental Therapeutics and Pathophysiology Branch and other NIH units, and from university psychiatry and psychology departments in Germany and the USA. The senior author's ketamine patents are a flag for closer reading of the review's favourable framing of ketamine therapy, not a reason to discount it; none of the 14 included studies is by the review's authors.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials of music against no music (and of patient-chosen against standard music) during subanaesthetic ketamine or esketamine treatment, with blinded assessment of dissociation, anxiety, tolerability and antidepressant response, pre-registered outcomes and enough participants to estimate effects; and a systematic review that appraises the procedural trials' risk of bias before pooling them.

domains.note: Registered protocol; five databases (Embase, PsycInfo and PsycArticles, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection) searched by a librarian to November 2022, updated December 2023, plus Google Scholar; explicit criteria; two reviewers screened independently at both levels after a pilot, and two extracted independently. Limits: English only; the search strings are in a supplement that is not part of the PMC author manuscript; whether the 1,191 Google Scholar full texts were screened in duplicate is not stated.
No appraisal of any included study; whether music was randomly allocated is stated for only one study, and case reports, qualitative studies and controlled trials are summarized alike.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the 14 included studies is by the review's authors; their own ketamine work is cited only for background.

Highlights, section 3.4 and the recommendations state benefits as findings while the Limitations say no conclusions can be drawn; a recommendation calls a benefit known on sources outside the included set; Kaelen et al. (2018) is credited with a causal effect it did not test.

domains.domain: Balance of favourable against null or unfavourable findings for music with ketamine
domains.note: Null and unfavourable results are reported in the body (no effect on emergence reactions; more dreams or emergence reactions with music; distortions felt as negative; a patient who stopped the music) but dropped from the Highlights and the closing summaries; the under-represented side is the null and unfavourable evidence.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A scoping review maps evidence and is not rated as a systematic review (round brief). Its search and selection are systematic and well reported, but it appraises none of the 14 studies and its summary statements outrun them, so the overall judgment follows the worst domains. Cite it for the size and shape of the evidence up to December 2023 (14 studies; 5 with ketamine or esketamine alone, only one of them comparing listening with no listening; no study comparing music with no music during subanaesthetic ketamine for depression) and as a pointer to primary studies. Do not cite it for any claim that music reduces dissociation, anxiety, pain or sedative needs with ketamine; such claims need the primary studies, appraised.

key_findings.finding: Methods: protocol registered a priori on the Open Science Framework and reported with PRISMA-ScR; five databases searched by a biomedical librarian, completed November 2022 and updated December 2023, English only, no date limit; supplementary Google Scholar search February and December 2023; two reviewers screened independently at title-abstract and full-text level and two extracted data independently.
key_findings.locator: 2.1. Protocol and Registration; 2.2. Information Sources and Search Strategy, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; 2.4. Selection of Sources of Evidence; 2.5. Data Collection Process…

key_findings.finding: Flow: 863 database records, 358 duplicates removed, 505 screened, 37 read in full, 9 included; Google Scholar 1,413 records, 222 duplicates, 1,191 read in full, 5 included; 14 studies in all, 5 with ketamine or esketamine alone and 9 with ketamine combined with other drugs.
key_findings.locator: 3.1. Selection of Sources of Evidence, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Figure 1 legend

key_findings.finding: Of the five ketamine-alone studies, only one compared a group that listened with a group that heard nothing (Kim et al., 2010): 46 children having cardiac catheterization under ketamine anaesthesia, 23 of whom heard recordings of their mothers' voices (musical in 12, non-musical in 8, mixed in 3) and had lower preoperative anxiety and fewer emergence reactions and less agitation than 23 who wore headphones with no recording. The others are a single-case report, a two-patient case report and two qualitative studies (17 and 12 people); for the 17-person study Table 1 records a control group without saying how many listened to music, and no music comparison is reported.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; 3.2.3. Music's Impact on Pediatric Anxiety, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Qualitative findings with ketamine or esketamine alone: in 17 people with treatment-resistant depression on oral esketamine, music was described as blocking distractions, anchoring them to reality and deepening internal exploration, while one participant stopped using it because it kept him tied to the outside world; in 12 people given ketamine in a trial for alcohol use disorder, all who listened to music had auditory distortions (shifts in speed and pitch), felt as positive or negative depending on their state.
key_findings.locator: 3.2.1. Music as a Distraction/For Noise Reduction and as an Aid to Internal Exploration; 3.2.5. Adding More Depth to the Experience; Table 1
key_findings.note: 'One participant stopped' follows Table 1; the review's text (3.2.1, 1st paragraph) says some participants felt music kept them tethered to the outside world.

key_findings.finding: Case reports: one woman with depression on esketamine nasal spray found that music of her choice helped with dissociation, confusion and anxiety (the presence of staff also helped); two patients with bipolar depression tolerated dissociation better when they heard preferred music in later intravenous ketamine infusions, which the review notes may reflect becoming used to the infusions.
key_findings.locator: 3.2.2. Mitigating Dissociation and Anxiety; 3.2.4. Enhancing Tolerability and Treatment Outcomes; 3.4, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Combination studies (ketamine with other sedatives or analgesics, in procedures or, in one study, air medical transport): music went with less intraoperative sedation, lower anxiety, pain or fear, and lower drug use in most; one trial found no effect on emergence reactions (Kumar et al., 1992), and another found more dreams or emergence reactions with music but no unpleasant dreams, against 10 controls with unpleasant dreams (Ambesh et al., 1991). A ninth study had music in both arms.
key_findings.locator: 3.3. Studies Examining Music and Ketamine in Conjunction with Other Substances, 1st to 8th paragraphs; Table 2

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: few studies, so no associations could be investigated and no conclusions drawn; English only; most studies concern anaesthetic use; the ketamine-alone studies were small, lacked quantitative analysis and proper controls; they call for randomized controlled trials and for offering patients the option of no music.
key_findings.locator: 5.0. Limitations and Future Directions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The review ends with recommendations for clinicians (inform patients that effects of music are exploratory and not universal; let them choose music, preferably without vocals; allow them to stop it; adjust lighting, eye covering, headphones and volume), drawn partly from sources outside the 14 included studies.
key_findings.locator: 4.0. Guidelines to Consider When Adding Music to Ketamine/Esketamine Therapy

reporting_issues.issue: De Araújo Azi et al. (2021): Table 2 gives 53 patients who heard music and 54 controls (and names 54 controls in its control column), while the text gives 53 who did not listen and 54 who did; the age range is 18–65 in the table but 19–65 and 18–66 for the two groups in the text.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Table 2, de Araújo Azi row; 3.3, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Group sizes are reversed between table and text; check the primary paper before citing numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: Ambesh et al. (1991): Table 2 says the music group had a higher incidence of dreams, while the text says music increased the incidence of emergence reactions.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Table 2, Ambesh row; 3.3, 5th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Which outcome rose with music is unclear; it matters because emergence reactions are the main adverse effect of ketamine anaesthesia.

reporting_issues.issue: Kim et al. (2010) is included, and described as parental voices singing familiar songs, although by Table 1 only 12 of 23 maternal-voice recordings were musical (8 non-musical, 3 mixed), while the eligibility criteria exclude non-music sounds.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Table 1, Kim row; 2.3, 2nd paragraph; 3.2.3, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The only controlled ketamine-alone study tested familiar voices, mostly but not only singing, rather than music.

reporting_issues.issue: Breeksema et al. (2022): the text describes 17 people who listened to calming music during treatment, while Table 1 says there was a control group but not how many listened to music and how many did not.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), 3.2.1; Table 1, Breeksema row
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of people whose accounts concern music is unknown, and the control group's role is not explained; no music comparison is reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction and Table 3 credit Kaelen et al. (2018) with showing that music improved psilocybin outcomes in treatment-resistant depression and enhanced brain emotional responses, and cite LSD studies in healthy volunteers (Kaelen et al., 2015, 2016, by their titles) for music acting synergistically with psychedelics to improve outcomes in major depressive disorder.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), 1.0. Introduction, 2nd paragraph; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: Kaelen et al. (2018) correlated interview-rated music experience with outcome in 19 patients who all heard music and took no brain measures (card sc_kaelen_2018); these statements should not be repeated from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 4.0 says calming instrumental music is known to promote introspection and positive outcomes in ketamine sessions, citing Allen and Ivester (2018), Kikkeri et al. (2021), Lersch et al. (2021) and Schenberg (2018), none of them among the included studies; the Introduction lists Allen and Ivester and Lersch et al. among studies in which music's effects were neither studied nor reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), 4.0, 2nd recommendation; 1.0. Introduction, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The recommendation's evidence base contradicts the review's own description of those sources.

reporting_issues.issue: The Highlights state as findings that music reduces dissociation and anxiety and boosts tolerability with ketamine alone and reduces sedative load in combinations, while the Limitations say no associations could be investigated and no conclusions drawn.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers of the Highlights alone would take case reports and unappraised trials as established effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The search strategy is said to be in a Supplement, but the PMC author manuscript lists no supplementary file; the OSF protocol is linked (not read).
reporting_issues.consequence: The search cannot be reproduced from this source; no finding of the card depends on the supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: Pereira et al. (2021): Table 1 says music was played after the esketamine dose, during the clinic stay, while the text says it was heard during the esketamine treatments. Table 1 also calls the phase after the double-blind period 'open-label ketamine', apparently a slip for esketamine.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Table 1, Pereira row; 3.2.2
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the timing of music relative to the dose is unclear for this case.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract and the Introduction (4th paragraph) say the extant studies explored music with ketamine or esketamine in healthy volunteers as well as in patients, but none of the 14 included studies involved healthy volunteers: by Tables 1 and 2, all were in patients in clinical or trial settings.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Abstract; 1.0. Introduction, 4th paragraph; Tables 1 and 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's evidence is all in patients in clinical or trial settings (recreational settings were excluded by design); it cannot be cited for healthy volunteers or for use outside clinics.
